after: `srcset` can offer the same picture in different sizes. After each filename, a width such as `320w` states how many pixels wide that file is. It describes the file, not how wide it must look on the page.

`sizes` tells the browser how wide you expect the picture to appear. `100vw` means the full width of the page-viewing area. This is a hint for choosing a file; it does not resize the picture by itself. A real page’s layout should match the hint.

This example offers two widths of the same ridge picture. ```html ``` `src` is the fallback. `srcset` lists the 320- and 640-pixel files. The sizes hint says full width at 600 pixels or less, and 320 pixels on wider views. The browser uses that hint and screen detail to choose a file.

If you change `100vw` to `50vw`, the narrow-screen hint becomes half the viewing width. At a width of 500 pixels, that means 250 pixels. It still does not guarantee which file the browser will choose.

Add the image with both supplied ridge files. Use the exact srcset and sizes values from the example, keeping `100vw` for this task. Include the dimensions and alt text. Run the checks. To view the downloaded files, keep both SVG files beside the HTML file.
